rv.q: The Last Ship is an awesome spectacle and a heartfelt one too. It is a personal project, which gives it integrity.
The Last Ship ends up as an engaging depiction of a community in crisis.

As it briefly docks at Theatre Royal Drury Lane, with Sting himself in a lead role, it’s worth saluting the venture (and applauding its decent tunes), but it lacks a sufficient feel-good factor and goes overboard in its scale.
It has a great deal going for it and is far from a mere vanity project for a man who has achieved greatness many times over in a successful career spanning close to 50 years.
The Last Ship may not entirely overcome the structural challenges that have followed it throughout its long journey to the West End, but this production comes closer than ever.
Sting gives a spirited performance as the illness-riddled foreman Jackie White, bringing his real-life experience living in Wallsend and landing the show some-much needed heart.
At nearly three hours, it is perhaps a little long, but it is full of heart and conviction.
It is not a perfect voyage, but a sail on The Last Ship is far from heading for the rocks.
Overall, despite its narrative flaws, I would still recommend checking this show out before its strictly limited run concludes.

cn.t: Sting's autobiographical shipbuilding musical receives mixed reviews, with critics praising its spectacular production design and heartfelt story but finding the drama lacking in emotional depth and narrative momentum.
